opus-5.5.text:
I think the core thing is that being smart in the sense of "can answer hard questions" or "can do a well-specified task in an hour" isn't the same as being able to do a job. When you look at what current models are actually like, they're really impressive on contained tasks. You give them a self-contained coding problem or a tricky math question and they'll often do better than a pretty strong human. But most of the economically valuable work humans do isn't like that. It's long-horizon, it's messy, it involves figuring out what the task even is, and it involves building up a lot of context over weeks or months.

So one big piece is what I'd call learning on the job. A human employee who joins a company is kind of mediocre at first, but over a few months they absorb an enormous amount of tacit knowledge: how the codebase is structured, which people know what, what the actual priorities are versus what's written down. Current models mostly don't do that. Each time you start a new context, they're back to square one, and in-context learning, while real, seems to degrade over very long contexts and doesn't seem to match what a human gets from months of experience. So sample efficiency and continual learning feel like a real bottleneck, not just a detail.

A second piece is agency and error correction over long tasks. Models make mistakes, and so do humans, but humans are pretty good at noticing "wait, this isn't working, let me step back." Models tend to get stuck in loops, or confidently go down a wrong path, or they declare success when they haven't succeeded. On a ten-minute task that matters less. On a multi-week project, small per-step error rates compound, and you need robust self-correction to get anywhere.

And a third is what I'd loosely call judgment or taste: knowing which direction is promising, which experiment is worth running, when something is good enough. That's harder to train because it's harder to get a clean reward signal for it.

Now, I don't want to overstate this. I think it's quite plausible these gaps close faster than people expect, and the trend on task length models can handle has been improving fast. Maybe scaling plus more RL on agentic tasks just handles a lot of it. But I'm skeptical of the simple story that because models ace benchmarks and seem really smart in conversation, full replacement of human workers is right around the corner. There's a meaningful gap between "smart" and "can autonomously do the job," and I think we don't yet know exactly how hard that gap is to cross.

r001.rationale: It identifies learning on the job, including absorbing tacit knowledge over months, as a capability current models lack.

r002.rationale: It contrasts models’ limited learning from context with humans’ gains from months of experience, then names sample efficiency as a bottleneck.

r003.rationale: It says in-context learning degrades over long contexts, but does not distinguish retrieving information from synthesizing it across the context window.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing I'd push on is that "smart" and "good at tasks" are doing a lot of work in that sentence, and they're kind of hiding the hard part.

When people picture a model replacing a human, they often picture something like: the model is as good as the human at the core skill — writing the code, drafting the memo, whatever. And current models are honestly already pretty close to that on a lot of narrow, well-scoped things. If you give them a clear task with a clear spec and a feedback loop, they do well. That's what benchmarks measure, and that's why benchmarks look so impressive.

But that's not what a job is. A job is mostly a bunch of stuff that isn't the core skill. It's figuring out what the task even is. It's noticing that the thing you were asked to do is subtly wrong and going back to the person. It's holding context over weeks and months — remembering that this customer is annoyed, that this part of the codebase is fragile, that your manager cares about X but says Y. It's recovering gracefully when something goes sideways instead of confidently barrelling on. And it's being trusted to do all of that without someone checking your work every twenty minutes.

So my scepticism is less "the models aren't smart enough" and more that there are a few specific bottlenecks that smartness-on-a-benchmark doesn't straightforwardly buy you.

One is long-horizon agency. The models are much better at short tasks than long ones, and the length of task they can reliably handle has been growing — but it's growing from a pretty low base. A lot of human work is effectively one very long task with no clean checkpoints.

Another is what you might call reliability or robustness. A human who's 95% reliable on a step is fine because they notice the 5% and fix it. A model that's 95% reliable but doesn't notice its own failures compounds that error across every step of a long task, and you end up with something that's useless without supervision. And if you need supervision, you haven't replaced the human — you've changed their job.

And then there's the whole category of stuff around context, taste, and knowing the organisation. A lot of what makes a senior person valuable is tacit knowledge that no one ever wrote down. Models don't currently have a great way to acquire that, partly because they don't learn on the job the way people do. Every session they start more or less from scratch, plus whatever you managed to stuff into the context window.

Now, I want to be clear — I don't think any of these are fundamental barriers. I expect them to get solved. I'm actually fairly bullish on timelines compared to a lot of people. But I think the path from "scores great on evals" to "actually does the job" runs through these specific bottlenecks, and progress on them is somewhat decoupled from progress on raw capability. You could imagine a world where the models get a lot smarter on paper and you still don't see mass replacement for a while, because the agency and reliability stuff lags. And conversely, you could see fairly modest capability gains that unlock a lot once those pieces click into place.

So when I'm sceptical, it's really scepticism about the inference "it's smart, therefore it'll replace people soon," not scepticism that it'll eventually happen.

r001.rationale: The response says models do not currently learn on the job the way people do and presents that as a bottleneck to doing the job and replacing workers.

r002.rationale: It does not compare how sample-efficiently AIs and humans learn tasks.

r003.rationale: It mentions context windows but does not distinguish retrieving information from synthesizing information across the window.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a pretty big gap between being able to do a task when someone has specified exactly what they want, and being able to replace a person in a job. A person is often figuring out what needs doing, noticing when something has gone wrong, and deciding when to ask for help. They also have a lot of context that isn’t necessarily written down anywhere.

So you could have a model that’s very impressive on a benchmark, or that gives you a great answer in a short interaction, but that still needs enough supervision that handing it an entire job doesn’t work very well. If it makes a consequential mistake occasionally, and you need a human to check everything to catch those mistakes, that can substantially reduce the value of the automation.

I don’t think this is an argument that LLMs fundamentally can’t replace humans. It’s more that “the model is smart” doesn’t by itself tell you whether it can reliably carry out a long sequence of actions in a messy environment. You need to look at that capability directly, including how much human assistance it takes.

r001.rationale: The response describes figuring out what needs doing and handling long sequences of actions, but does not identify learning on the job as a capability LLMs need.

r002.rationale: It discusses supervision and human checking, but does not compare how efficiently AIs and humans learn tasks from examples or experience.

r003.rationale: It mentions context that may not be written down, but does not distinguish retrieving information from synthesizing information across a context window.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a distinction between being able to do a task when it’s clearly specified and being able to replace someone in a job. A job often involves figuring out what needs to happen, noticing when something has gone wrong, and following through over a long period of time. You can be very good at answering individual questions and still struggle with that broader process.

Reliability is a big part of this. If a model does something impressive on a task, that tells you it has some relevant capability. But if you want to hand it a project and come back a week later, you need it to handle a whole series of decisions, including situations where it’s confused or where the obvious approach doesn’t work. Small failure rates can become a substantial problem over that many steps.

That doesn’t mean these problems won’t get solved. I expect systems to improve, and you can compensate for some weaknesses with tools and oversight. But I’m sceptical of jumping straight from ‘these models are very smart’ to ‘therefore they can replace humans across a broad range of work.’ There’s additional evidence you’d want about whether they can actually carry out that work autonomously.

r001.rationale: The response discusses identifying what needs to happen and following through, but does not identify learning on the job as a capability LLMs need.

r002.rationale: It mentions reliability and small failure rates, but makes no comparison of how efficiently AIs and humans learn tasks from examples.

r003.rationale: It does not distinguish retrieving information from a context window from synthesizing information across it.
